description: Stirling Vanguards is an interdisciplinary team of dedicated Software Engineering and Computing Science students from the University of Stirling RAK Campus. United by a passion for space exploration and data-driven problem-solving, our team combines technical expertise in full-stack development, GIS mapping, and data analytics to build innovative tools for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
Vanguard Atlas is an open-source planetary analog comparison tool that identifies where on Earth to test hardware and field procedures for permanent Moon and Mars base operations, and shows exactly where the analogy breaks down.

The challenge asks us to identify Earth locations that analog permanent Moon base sites and Mars. The core problem we solved is that no single Earth site replicates another world, and collapsing terrain, thermal, geological, and subsurface conditions into one "similarity score" hides the trade-offs mission planners most need to see. Vanguard Atlas instead scores each Earth analog against a real orbital target footprint one dimension at a time, never blended.

Using a reproducible Python pipeline, we scored eight terrestrial analogs against two targets, the Lunar South Pole and Jezero Crater, across four dimensions, producing 16 site-target pairs with per-dimension scores, explicit confidence badges, documented strengths, and specific breakdown limits. Terrain metrics come from 30 m Copernicus GLO-30 DEM tiles on Earth, 240 m LRO LOLA on the Moon, and 463 m MGS MOLA on Mars; thermal, geological, and subsurface baselines come from WorldClim, LRO Diviner, MGS TES, and published USGS/PDS catalogs.

The result is a zero-backend interactive web atlas where engineers can compare candidates per dimension, see exactly why a site matched or failed, and know what Earth cannot replicate vacuum, partial gravity, radiation, and 40 K polar cold traps.
details:
What does it do / how does it work?​

Vanguard Atlas is a static web application that compares terrestrial analog field sites against extraterrestrial target footprints across four independent physical dimensions — terrain, thermal, geology, and subsurface — and never blends them into a single similarity score.

A reproducible Python pipeline does the work. Target raster data is ingested directly from NASA Planetary Data System archives: LRO LOLA GDRDSM (240 m, lunar south polar slope map) and MGS MOLA MEGDR (463 m, Mars topography), both decoded by custom readers that convert raw binary PDS images into slope statistics. Earth terrain features are extracted from Copernicus DEM GLO-30 30 m tiles using a 5 km circular footprint per site. Thermal baselines come from WorldClim v2.1 on Earth, LRO Diviner on the Moon, and MGS TES / Mars 2020 MEDA on Mars. Geology and subsurface baselines draw on published USGS, CRISM, Diviner/Mini-RF, and cave/pit catalogs. Each Earth site is then scored against each target dimension by feature-wise similarity using configurable tolerances, passed through a confidence model that downgrades scores when data is catalog-based or resolution-mismatched, and exported as contract-valid JSON records.

The web app loads those records at runtime and renders them: interactive maps per target body, ranked tables sortable by any single dimension, multi-axis radar comparisons, and detailed site cards stating what a place is good for, where the analogy stops working, and what you could actually test there.

What benefits does it have?​

Terrestrial analog selection is currently guesswork. Engineers pick sites by reputation, and a single composite score hides the exact mismatch that matters — a site with perfect terrain can have completely wrong thermal or mineralogical behavior. Vanguard Atlas surfaces those trade-offs explicitly, so a team testing rover mobility on flat slopes is never misled by a site that fails thermally. Every result carries a confidence badge and named breakdown limits, which keeps methodological honesty visible in the interface rather than buried in an appendix.

What is the intended impact?​

Every major Moon and Mars mission plan includes analog field campaigns. We intend Vanguard Atlas to be the starting point for that selection: open, reproducible, and backed by documented NASA data with per-dataset licensing and access dates. Anyone can add a new target raster or candidate site and get a comparable, confidence-tagged result.

Creative tools, coding, hardware, or software used?​

Python (pandas, numpy, PyYAML, jsonschema, pytest) for ingestion, feature extraction, scoring, confidence, validation, and export. Vanilla JavaScript ES modules with MapLibre GL for the front end — no framework, no backend, no build step. GitHub Actions for automated deployment to GitHub Pages. No custom hardware; all data is open NASA/ESA/JAXA orbital and ground archives.

What factors did your team consider?​

We deliberately avoided a single composite score, because averaging erases exactly the trade-offs the challenge asks us to expose. We also prioritized honesty over polish: all 16 site-target pairs are currently tagged low confidence because the target profiles rely on catalog and proxy data that remains unverified, and we say so in the interface. Automated validation checks our scoring against published analog literature, including positive controls (Atacama, Death Valley, Haughton, McMurdo) and negative controls (Hawaiian shield volcanoes) to confirm the pipeline rejects false matches.
